_schema: tn-assessment-specialist / tcap-item-writer-v2 schema (Government adaptation). Scaled Unit 2 MCQ bank across DOK 1–3. Classroom-formative · pre-field-test.
subject: government

items.dokRationale: Recalls which listed act is a legal duty.
items.bloomsRationale: Student recognizes a fact from the standard.
items.question: Which action is a legal duty of U.S. citizens rather than a voluntary act?

options.A: Serving on a jury if summoned
options.B: Volunteering weekly at a food bank
options.C: Joining a political party campaign
options.D: Attending a city council meeting

distractorRationales.A: Correct — jury duty is a legal obligation when summoned.
distractorRationales.B: Voluntary service, not a legal duty.
distractorRationales.D: Voluntary civic engagement, not a duty.

items.dokRationale: Explains why a duty matters, not just recall.
items.question: Why is paying taxes considered essential to the well-being of the nation?

options.A: It replaces the need for any voting
options.B: It funds public services and national defense
options.C: It guarantees a citizen a public office
options.D: It removes the duty to obey the laws

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — taxes do not replace voting.
distractorRationales.B: Correct — taxes fund shared services and defense.
distractorRationales.C: Plausible error — taxes do not buy office.
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — taxes do not remove legal duties.

items.dokRationale: Recalls a voting requirement.
items.question: Which requirement must a person meet to register to vote in Tennessee?

options.A: Belong to a political party
options.B: Own property in the county
options.C: Be eighteen years of age
options.D: Pass a national civics exam

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — party membership is not required.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — no property requirement exists.
distractorRationales.C: Correct — 18, U.S. citizenship, and residency are required.
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — civics/literacy tests are prohibited.

items.dokRationale: Explains a consequence of non-voting.
items.question: What is one likely impact when many eligible citizens choose not to vote?

options.A: Jury duty is no longer legally required
options.B: The winning candidate must resign at once
options.C: Taxes are automatically canceled that year
options.D: Results represent fewer people's real views

distractorRationales.A: Near miss — an unrelated duty.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — no resignation results.
distractorRationales.D: Correct — low turnout narrows whose views count.

items.dokRationale: Explains the civic meaning of service.
items.question: Serving in the military or performing alternative service is best described as:

options.A: a way to serve the nation
options.B: a punishment for breaking the law
options.C: a requirement to hold any job
options.D: a substitute for paying all taxes

distractorRationales.A: Correct — service is a civic contribution.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — it is not a punishment.
distractorRationales.C: Plausible error — not a job requirement.
distractorRationales.D: Plausible error — it does not replace taxes.

items.dokRationale: Recalls the U.S. party structure.
items.question: The United States is best described as having what kind of party system?

options.A: A one-party system
options.B: A two-party system
options.C: A no-party system
options.D: A four-party system

distractorRationales.A: Near miss — describes authoritarian states.
distractorRationales.B: Correct — two major parties dominate U.S. politics.
distractorRationales.D: Plausible error — not four dominant parties.

items.dokRationale: Explains a distinction between two processes.
items.question: What is the main difference between an open and a closed primary?

options.A: How many candidates may enter it
options.B: When the votes are finally counted up
options.C: Who may vote in the primary election
options.D: Where the polling places are set up

distractorRationales.A: Near miss — candidate count is unrelated.
distractorRationales.B: Plausible error — timing is not the difference.
distractorRationales.C: Correct — open lets any voter; closed limits to party members.
distractorRationales.D: Plausible error — location is not the difference.

items.dokRationale: Recalls the definition of a caucus.
items.question: In the presidential nomination process, a caucus is a:

options.A: tax paid by each new candidate here
options.B: national holiday set for all voters
options.C: court that settles election disputes
options.D: meeting where members pick a candidate

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — not a tax.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — not a holiday.
distractorRationales.D: Correct — a local meeting to select a candidate.

items.dokRationale: Analyzes a cause of the two-party structure.
items.question: Why do winner-take-all elections help keep the two-party system in place?

options.A: Small parties rarely win any seats outright
options.B: A law bans the forming of new parties
options.C: A firm rule requires two parties
options.D: A tax is charged to every third party

distractorRationales.A: Correct — winner-take-all shuts out small parties, favoring two.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — no ban on parties.
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — no such tax.

items.dokRationale: Explains a distinction between election types.
items.question: How does a general election differ from a primary election?

options.A: It selects each party's own single nominee
options.B: It chooses officials between parties' nominees
options.C: It counts only the early caucus results
options.D: It is open only to elected officials now

distractorRationales.A: Near miss — that describes a primary.
distractorRationales.B: Correct — the general election decides among nominees.
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — general elections are open to voters.

items.dokRationale: Recalls the purpose of a poll.
items.question: A public opinion poll is used mainly to:

options.A: write the new laws for the states
options.B: elect the president of the country now
options.C: measure what people think about issues
options.D: count the votes on election day here

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — polls do not make law.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — polls do not elect anyone.
distractorRationales.D: Near miss — vote counting is separate.

items.dokRationale: Explains how a design choice affects data.
items.question: How can the wording of a poll question affect its results?

options.A: Only the poll's date changes the results
options.B: Wording has no effect on the responses
options.C: Longer questions get more correct answers
options.D: Biased wording can push certain answers

distractorRationales.A: Plausible error — date is not the driver.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — wording clearly matters.
distractorRationales.C: Plausible error — length is not the issue.
distractorRationales.D: Correct — loaded wording skews responses.

items.dokRationale: Explains the meaning of a key term.
items.question: What does the term 'media bias' describe?

options.A: Slanted coverage that favors one side
options.B: The total number of news channels now
options.C: A tax placed on all of the newspapers
options.D: The rule that reporters must go vote

distractorRationales.A: Correct — bias is one-sided coverage.
distractorRationales.B: Near miss — channel count is unrelated.
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — no such rule.

items.dokRationale: Explains a civic function of the media.
items.question: One important role of the media in a democracy is to:

options.A: choose the winners of every election
options.B: inform the public about government actions
options.C: collect the taxes from all news readers
options.D: write the laws that are passed by Congress

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — media does not elect officials.
distractorRationales.B: Correct — the media informs citizens (a watchdog role).
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — media does not legislate.

items.dokRationale: Analyzes how wording biases a result.
items.question: A poll asks, 'Do you support wasteful government spending?' Why might its results mislead?

options.A: The sample was clearly far too large
options.B: Polls cannot measure any real opinion
options.C: The loaded word 'wasteful' invites a No
options.D: People answer every poll the same way

distractorRationales.A: Plausible error — sample size is not the flaw.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — polls can measure opinion.
distractorRationales.C: Correct — the loaded word biases the answer.
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — responses vary.

items.dokRationale: Recalls a form of participation.
items.question: Which of these is a way citizens participate in the political process?

options.A: Buying groceries at the local store
options.B: Watching television purely for fun
options.C: Paying a monthly cell phone bill
options.D: Signing a petition for a cause

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — a private activity.
distractorRationales.B: Near miss — entertainment is not participation.
distractorRationales.D: Correct — petitioning is political participation.

items.dokRationale: Recalls the definition of lobbying.
items.question: Lobbying is best defined as:

options.A: trying to influence officials' decisions
options.B: voting once in a national election
options.C: serving a full sentence in a prison
options.D: paying yearly taxes to the government

distractorRationales.A: Correct — lobbying seeks to influence officials.
distractorRationales.B: Near miss — voting is separate.
distractorRationales.D: Plausible error — a duty, not lobbying.

items.dokRationale: Explains the purpose of direct-democracy tools.
items.question: What is the shared purpose of an initiative, a referendum, and a recall?

options.A: To choose the U.S. Supreme Court justices
options.B: To let citizens shape laws more directly
options.C: To collect extra taxes from the states
options.D: To declare a war on other foreign nations

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — courts are unrelated.
distractorRationales.B: Correct — these tools give voters direct influence.
distractorRationales.D: Misconception — unrelated to war powers.

items.dokRationale: Explains how a tool broadens participation.
items.question: How does a recall election increase citizen participation?

options.A: It bans all of the future elections
options.B: It doubles the yearly salary of officials
options.C: It lets voters remove an official early
options.D: It appoints new judges without a vote

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — it does not ban elections.
distractorRationales.B: Misconception — unrelated to pay.
distractorRationales.C: Correct — voters can remove an official before term's end.
distractorRationales.D: Near miss — appointments are separate.

items.dokRationale: Explains the category of two participation forms.
items.question: Demonstrating and petitioning are protected as forms of:

options.A: running a small private family business
options.B: paying the required yearly federal taxes
options.C: serving on a local county trial jury
options.D: citizens expressing their political views

distractorRationales.A: Misconception — unrelated economic activity.
distractorRationales.B: Near miss — a duty, not expression.
distractorRationales.C: Near miss — a duty, not expression.
distractorRationales.D: Correct — protest and petition are political expression.
